A print unit is designed with a defined transport path that establishes the direction along which stock materials are conveyed through the unit during operation. This transport path serves as the fundamental reference for the arrangement and orientation of the unit's internal components.

Central to this configuration is a suction system comprising at least two suction boxes. Each of these suction boxes is equipped with inlet openings that are oriented to at least partially face the direction of stock transport, thereby optimizing airflow interaction with the moving stock as it passes through the print unit.

In the transverse direction—perpendicular to the direction of stock transport—the inlet openings of the suction boxes collectively define an overall inlet length. The suction boxes themselves are arranged side by side along the transverse direction, forming a coordinated array across the working width of the print unit. Notably, each suction box is constructed to allow independent removal from the print unit. This means that any individual suction box can be extracted for maintenance, inspection, or replacement without requiring the removal or disturbance of adjacent suction boxes, thereby simplifying service procedures and minimizing downtime.

Despite their modular and independently removable design, all suction boxes within the print unit can be integrated into a single common suction line. # Print Unit Stock Transport System with Modular Suction Box Configuration

## Technical Background

In modern printing equipment, particularly in high-speed web-fed printing applications, the reliable transport of substrate stock through the print unit is a critical engineering challenge. The stock material, whether paper, film, or other flexible substrates, must be guided consistently across the entire working width of the print unit to ensure uniform print quality and prevent misalignment, wrinkling, or tension variations that could compromise the printing process.

## Suction Box Configuration

The present print unit addresses these stock transport requirements through an innovative arrangement of suction boxes positioned to control and stabilize the substrate as it moves through the printing zone. The system employs **at least two suction boxes**, each incorporating inlet openings that face directly into the transport direction of the stock material. This orientation ensures that the suction airflow is optimally positioned to interact with the moving substrate, providing the necessary holding force to maintain proper stock positioning and tension.

Collectively, these suction boxes are engineered to span an **inlet length covering 80% of the working width** in the transverse direction—that is, the direction perpendicular to the stock's travel path. This substantial coverage ensures that suction forces are applied consistently across nearly the entire width of the substrate, minimizing the risk of localized instability, lateral drift, or uneven tension that could otherwise result from gaps in suction coverage. By achieving this high percentage of width coverage, the design provides robust and uniform control over the stock material throughout its passage through the print unit.

## Modular Independence and Removability

A key innovative feature of this configuration is that **each suction box is independently removable** from its adjacent boxes. Rather than constructing the suction system as a single, monolithic unit spanning the entire working width, the design deliberately segments the suction coverage into discrete, self-contained modules. Each of these individual suction boxes can be detached, extracted, or otherwise separated from the neighboring units without requiring the disassembly or disruption of the adjacent boxes.

This modular architecture represents a deliberate design choice that prioritizes serviceability and maintenance flexibility. In traditional single-unit suction systems, any malfunction, wear, or damage affecting even a small portion of the suction mechanism typically necessitates the removal or servicing of the entire assembly—a process that can result in extended downtime and increased maintenance complexity. By contrast, the segmented approach described here allows maintenance personnel to isolate and address issues in a specific suction box without affecting the operational status of neighboring units.

## Common Suction Line Connectivity

Despite their independent, modular construction, all suction boxes within the system are **connectable to a common suction line**. This shared pneumatic infrastructure ensures that, during normal operation, all suction boxes function as a cohesive system, drawing from the same vacuum source to generate consistent suction pressure across the entire covered width. The common suction line serves as the unifying element that allows individually modular components to operate together seamlessly, providing uniform suction performance despite the physical separation of the boxes themselves.

This connectivity design requires careful engineering to ensure that when one suction box is removed for maintenance or replacement, the remaining boxes can continue to operate effectively, potentially through valve mechanisms, sealing systems, or pressure-regulating components that maintain suction line integrity even when one segment is temporarily disconnected.

## Advantages of the Modular Design

The combination of independent removability with shared suction line connectivity yields several significant operational advantages:

**Enhanced Serviceability**: Maintenance technicians can perform targeted repairs, cleaning, or replacement of individual suction boxes without the need to shut down or disassemble the entire suction system. This significantly reduces the complexity and time required for routine maintenance procedures.

**Reduced Downtime**: Because neighboring suction boxes remain undisturbed during the servicing of a single unit, the overall print unit can potentially continue limited operation or be returned to full operation more quickly after maintenance activities, minimizing costly production interruptions.

**Consistent Suction Performance**: Despite the modular and segmented construction, the system is engineered to maintain uniform suction performance across the entire 80% working width coverage. This ensures that print quality and substrate handling remain consistent even as individual components are serviced or replaced over time.

**Simplified Component Management**: The modular nature of the suction boxes allows for easier inventory management, as individual boxes can be stocked as replacement parts, and only the specific malfunctioning unit needs to be replaced rather than an entire integrated system.

**Scalability and Adaptability**: This design approach may also facilitate adaptation to different working widths or configurations, as the modular boxes could potentially be reconfigured or supplemented to address varying production requirements.

## Conclusion

This modular suction box design represents a thoughtful engineering solution to the dual challenges of maintaining effective stock transport control and ensuring practical serviceability in print unit operations. By segmenting the suction coverage into independently removable units while maintaining connectivity to a common suction line, the system achieves the seemingly competing goals of comprehensive, uniform suction performance and simplified, efficient maintenance procedures—ultimately contributing to improved operational efficiency and reduced maintenance-related downtime in printing operations.

# The Word "The"

"The" is one of the most fundamental words in the English language, serving as the definite article that precedes nouns to indicate specificity. Despite its brevity—just three letters—it holds the distinction of being the most frequently used word in written and spoken English, appearing far more often than any other word in the language.

## Grammatical Function

The primary role of "the" is to specify that a noun refers to something particular or already known to the listener or reader. For example, saying "the book" implies a specific book, perhaps one previously mentioned or contextually understood, as opposed to "a book," which refers to any unspecified book. This distinction between definite and indefinite articles is a cornerstone of English grammar and helps convey precision in communication.

## Historical Origins

The word traces its roots back to Old English, where it developed from demonstrative pronouns and adjectives such as "se," "seo," and "þæt." Over centuries, these forms evolved and merged into the single word "the" that we use today. This evolution reflects broader patterns in language simplification, where multiple grammatical forms often consolidate into more streamlined structures over time.

## Linguistic Significance

Linguists study "the" not only for its grammatical function but also for what it reveals about cognitive processes in language comprehension. The use of definite articles varies significantly across languages—some, like Russian and Japanese, lack articles altogether, while others have complex systems of gendered or case-based articles. This variation offers insight into how different languages encode specificity and shared knowledge between speakers.

## Cultural and Practical Presence

Beyond grammar, "the" appears in countless idioms, titles, and phrases, often used to add emphasis or importance—consider phrases like "the one and only" or "the best." Its ubiquity makes it a word most native speakers use unconsciously, rarely pausing to consider its function, yet its consistent presence underscores its critical role in constructing clear and meaningful sentences.

In essence, "the" exemplifies how small words can carry substantial grammatical weight, shaping the way we specify, emphasize, and understand the world through language.

counterfactuals.output:
# Technical Specification: Vacuum Suction Box Stock Stabilization System

## 1. Scope

This specification defines the design, performance, and interface requirements for a modular suction box assembly used to stabilize web or sheet stock during transport through a printing press. The system consists of multiple independently removable suction boxes connected to a shared vacuum manifold.

---

## 2. General Description

The suction box assembly stabilizes paper, film, or board stock as it travels across press sections (e.g., feeder, printing units, delivery) by applying negative pressure through perforated or slotted deck plates. Multiple suction boxes are arranged along the transport path and connected to a common suction (vacuum) line, while each box remains independently removable for maintenance, cleaning, or format changeover without disrupting the vacuum supply to adjacent boxes.

---

## 3. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| Suction Box | Individual chamber assembly that applies localized vacuum to the stock surface via a perforated deck |
| Common Suction Line | Shared vacuum manifold/header supplying multiple suction boxes |
| Deck Plate | Perforated or slotted top surface of the suction box in contact-proximity with the stock |
| Isolation Valve | Manual or automatic valve isolating an individual box from the common line |
| Quick-Disconnect (QD) Coupling | Tool-less or low-tool connector enabling rapid removal/installation of a box |

---

## 4. Functional Requirements

### 4.1 Stock Stabilization
- FR-1: Each suction box shall generate sufficient negative pressure to hold stock flat against the deck plate at rated press speeds up to **[X] m/min**.
- FR-2: Vacuum level at each box shall be independently adjustable within a range of **-2 kPa to -15 kPa** (gauge) to accommodate varying stock weights (e.g., 40–400 gsm).
- FR-3: The system shall maintain stable vacuum (±5% of setpoint) across the full operating speed range.

### 4.2 Modularity and Individual Removal
- FR-4: Each suction box shall be removable from the press frame and common suction line **without depressurizing or disassembling the common line**.
- FR-5: Removal and reinstallation of a single box shall be achievable by one technician in **≤ 5 minutes** using standard tools or tool-less mechanisms.
- FR-6: Removal of any single box shall not degrade vacuum performance in remaining boxes by more than **10%**.

### 4.3 Common Suction Line Interface
- FR-7: All suction boxes shall connect to a single shared vacuum header via individual branch lines.
- FR-8: Each branch line shall include an isolation valve (manual ball/butterfly or pneumatically actuated) positioned upstream of the QD coupling.
- FR-9: The isolation valve shall automatically close (or be interlocked to close) upon disconnection of a box to prevent vacuum loss/air ingress into the common line.

---

## 5. Mechanical Design Requirements

### 5.1 Suction Box Construction
- Material: Anodized aluminum or stainless steel (304/316) housing for corrosion resistance and low weight.
- Deck Plate: Interchangeable perforated stainless steel or polymer deck, hole pattern optimized per stock type (typical hole diameter 1.5–3 mm, open area 15–30%).
- Internal chamber shall include baffling to ensure uniform vacuum distribution across the deck surface (±10% variation across deck area).

### 5.2 Mounting and Removal Mechanism
- MR-1: Boxes shall mount on a common rail or frame system using a **cam-lock, quarter-turn, or spring-loaded latch** mechanism.
- MR-2: Positioning shall be self-aligning (guide pins or dowels) to ensure repeatable deck-to-stock gap tolerance of **± 0.5 mm**.
- MR-3: Each box shall weigh no more than **[X] kg** to permit single-person removal, or shall include integrated lift handles/assist points.

### 5.3 Common Suction Line
- Manifold Material: Stainless steel or reinforced PVC, rated for vacuum service to **-20 kPa** minimum.
- Manifold shall include:
  - Sizing sufficient to serve the maximum number of connected boxes without pressure drop exceeding 5% at full flow.
  - Drain/condensate ports at low points.
  - Access ports for pressure/vacuum instrumentation.
- Branch Connections: Quick-disconnect vacuum couplings (self-sealing type) rated for repeated connect/disconnect cycles (≥ 10,000 cycles) without leakage degradation.

---

## 6. Pneumatic/Vacuum System Requirements

| Parameter | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Vacuum Source | Centrifugal blower or vacuum pump, sized for total connected load + 20% margin |
| Common Line Vacuum Range | -5 kPa to -20 kPa adjustable |
| Individual Box Control | Local throttling valve or variable frequency drive (VFD) zoning per box or box group |
| Leak Rate (isolated, disconnected box) | ≤ 1% of rated flow when isolation valve closed |
| Filtration | Inline particulate filter upstream of vacuum source, rated to capture paper dust/fiber ≥ 90% at 10 micron |

---

## 7. Electrical/Control Requirements (if automated isolation valves used)

- Isolation valves shall be pneumatically or electrically actuated with a fail-closed configuration on loss of signal/power.
- Control system shall provide operator feedback (HMI or indicator light) showing:
  - Box connected/disconnected status
  - Vacuum level per zone
  - Fault/alarm on vacuum loss below threshold
- Safety interlock: Press shall not run at production speed if a required suction box is disconnected or isolated, unless explicitly overridden by operator for changeover mode.

---

## 8. Maintenance and Serviceability

- SR-1: Deck plates shall be removable for cleaning without removing the entire suction box (top-access fasteners, quarter-turn quick fasteners preferred).
- SR-2: All wear components (gaskets, seals, deck plates) shall be field-replaceable using standard hand tools.
- SR-3: QD couplings and isolation valves shall be accessible for inspection without requiring removal of adjacent boxes.
- SR-4: System shall support hot-swappable box replacement during scheduled stops without full vacuum system shutdown.

---

## 9. Performance Testing & Acceptance Criteria

| Test | Method | Acceptance Criteria |
|---|---|---|
| Vacuum Uniformity | Measure vacuum at 5 points across deck | ≤ ±10% deviation from mean |
| Box Removal Time | Timed removal/reinstall by single technician | ≤ 5 minutes |
| Isolation Leak Test | Disconnect box, measure common line pressure drop | ≤ 2% drop over 60 seconds |
| Stock Hold-Down Test | Run stock samples at max rated speed | Zero flutter/lift observed via high-speed camera |
| Cycle Durability | 10,000 connect/disconnect cycles on QD coupling | No leakage increase >5% from baseline |

---

## 10. Compliance and Standards

- Design shall comply with applicable machine safety standards (e.g., **ISO 12100**, **CE Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC**, or **ANSI B65.1** for printing press safety, as applicable to region).
- Electrical components shall meet **IEC 60204-1** (electrical equipment of machines).
- Materials in contact with stock shall be compatible with printing substrates (no contamination, static discharge per **IEC 61340** if applicable).

---

## 11. Documentation Deliverables

- Assembly and installation drawings
- Vacuum system schematic (P&ID)
- Maintenance and spare parts manual
- Operator quick-reference guide for box removal/reinstallation procedure
- Test/inspection certificates per Section 9

---

*Note: Bracketed values [X] denote parameters to be finalized based on specific press model, line speed, and stock specifications during detailed design phase.*

# Suction Box System Configuration – Transverse Arrangement

## 1. General Description

The suction box system, integral to the print unit's web-handling assembly, is configured along the transverse (cross-machine) axis to ensure uniform vacuum distribution across the operating width of the substrate. The system is engineered as a modular assembly to balance aerodynamic performance, structural integrity, and serviceability.

## 2. Inlet Length Specification

The suction box incorporates a primary vacuum inlet whose effective length is engineered to span a defined proportion of the overall box length, typically positioned centrally or at a designated reference point along the transverse axis. The inlet length is dimensioned to:

- Provide sufficient cross-sectional area for the required volumetric airflow at the specified static pressure differential
- Minimize localized pressure drop gradients that could induce non-uniform suction distribution across the width
- Interface with the upstream ductwork or blower manifold via a flanged or gasketed connection sized to match the inlet cross-section

The inlet is typically centrally manifolded to promote symmetric pressure distribution toward the box extremities, though multi-inlet configurations may be employed for wider working widths to mitigate pressure decay over distance.

## 3. Working Width Coverage

The suction box is dimensioned such that its active perforated or slotted suction area corresponds to a specified percentage of the maximum working width of the print unit — commonly on the order of **90–100%** of nominal web width, with the precise value determined by:

- Edge-trim allowances and web-tracking tolerances
- Avoidance of suction effect beyond the substrate edge (which would otherwise induce false air leakage and vacuum loss)
- Coordination with the widest anticipated substrate format processed by the unit

This percentage is specified in the design documentation as a ratio of *effective suction width* to *maximum web width*, ensuring consistent hold-down or transfer force across all qualified substrate widths.

## 4. Modular Segmentation

To accommodate varying web widths and to enable independent zone control, the suction box is often segmented into discrete transverse modules (zones). Each module:

- Is independently valved or damper-controlled to permit selective activation/deactivation corresponding to the active web width
- Maintains a standardized module width to allow interchangeability and scalability across different press configurations
- Is sealed against adjacent modules via gasketed interfaces to prevent inter-zone air leakage

## 5. Maintenance Access Configuration

The modular design is further structured to facilitate serviceability:

- Each transverse module is mounted on a removable or slide-out carriage, permitting individual withdrawal without disassembly of adjacent modules or the full suction box assembly
- Access panels or covers are provided on the top or front face of each module, secured via quick-release fasteners (e.g., quarter-turn latches or captive screws), enabling inspection and cleaning of the perforated deck plate and internal plenum
- Perforated/slotted top plates are designed as replaceable wear components, individually removable for cleaning of debris, fiber buildup, or coating residue without requiring full system shutdown beyond the isolation of the affected zone
- Isolation valves or dampers at each module inlet allow that zone to be taken offline for maintenance while adjacent zones remain in operation, minimizing production downtime

## 6. Summary

The transverse configuration of the suction box system thus integrates a centrally located, appropriately sized inlet; a suction footprint covering a defined percentage (typically 90–100%) of the working width; and a modular, zone-isolable architecture that supports both operational flexibility across varying web widths and streamlined maintenance access at the individual module level.

# Sheet Transport System with Independently Removable Suction Boxes

## Background

Below is draft patent-style language for the described printing machine stock transport system. This should be reviewed and refined by a registered patent attorney or agent before any filing, as claim language requires careful legal scrutiny to ensure proper scope and enforceability.

---

## Sample Specification Language

**Field of the Invention**

The present disclosure relates generally to sheet-fed printing machinery, and more particularly to a stock transport system employing suction-based sheet handling apparatus configured for modular maintenance and replacement.

**Summary**

In accordance with one embodiment, a stock transport system for a printing machine comprises a suction manifold defining a shared suction line, and at least two suction boxes fluidly coupled to the suction manifold. Each suction box is independently removable from the suction manifold without requiring removal or disassembly of the other suction box, and without interrupting suction supply to the remaining suction box or boxes.

**Detailed Description (illustrative embodiment)**

Referring to the drawings, a stock transport system 100 for conveying sheet stock through a printing machine is shown. The system 100 includes a suction source 110, a suction manifold 120 defining a shared suction line 122, and a plurality of suction boxes, including at least a first suction box 130 and a second suction box 140, each in fluid communication with the shared suction line 122.

In the illustrated embodiment, the first suction box 130 is coupled to the shared suction line 122 via a first quick-disconnect coupling 132, and the second suction box 140 is coupled to the shared suction line 122 via a second quick-disconnect coupling 142. Each of the quick-disconnect couplings 132, 142 may include a self-sealing valve element configured to close automatically upon disconnection of the respective suction box, thereby maintaining vacuum integrity in the shared suction line 122 during removal or servicing of either suction box.

Each suction box 130, 140 defines a plurality of apertures 134, 144, respectively, formed in an upper surface thereof, the apertures being configured to draw sheet stock into contact with a conveying surface via negative pressure communicated from the suction source 110 through the shared suction line 122.

In operation, the first suction box 130 and the second suction box 140 may be selectively and independently detached from the suction manifold 120—for example, for cleaning, inspection, repair, or replacement—without interrupting the supply of suction to the remaining suction box, and without requiring shutdown of the suction source 110 or depressurization of the shared suction line 122.

According to certain embodiments, at least one of the suction boxes 130, 140 is slidably mounted on a support rail 150 such that the suction box may be withdrawn in a direction transverse to a sheet travel path without disturbing the position or alignment of an adjacent suction box.

---

## Sample Claim Language

**Claim 1.**
A stock transport system for a printing machine, comprising:
a suction manifold defining a shared suction line;
a first suction box in fluid communication with the shared suction line via a first coupling; and
a second suction box in fluid communication with the shared suction line via a second coupling, the second suction box being spaced apart from the first suction box along a sheet travel path;
wherein each of the first suction box and the second suction box is independently removable from the suction manifold without removal of the other of the first suction box and the second suction box, and without interrupting suction communicated to the other of the first suction box and the second suction box.

**Claim 2.**
The stock transport system of claim 1, wherein at least one of the first coupling and the second coupling comprises a self-sealing valve configured to substantially seal the shared suction line upon disconnection of the corresponding suction box.

**Claim 3.**
The stock transport system of claim 1, wherein at least one of the first suction box and the second suction box is slidably mounted for removal in a direction transverse to the sheet travel path.

**Claim 4.**
The stock transport system of claim 1, wherein each of the first suction box and the second suction box defines a plurality of apertures configured to communicate negative pressure to an upper surface thereof for retaining sheet stock during transport.

**Claim 5.**
The stock transport system of claim 1, further comprising a suction source in fluid communication with the suction manifold, wherein the suction source remains in continuous operation during removal of either the first suction box or the second suction box.

---

### Notes for Refinement

A few things worth flagging as you develop this further:

- **Coupling mechanism specifics**: I used a generic "quick-disconnect coupling with self-sealing valve" — if your actual design uses a different mechanism (e.g., a manual shutoff valve, a cam-lock fitting, a bayonet connector), the claims should be tailored accordingly, since this is likely a key point of novelty.
- **Independent claims scope**: Consider whether you want a broader independent claim (covering just the modularity/independent-removability concept) with narrower dependent claims capturing the coupling details, or whether the self-sealing feature should be in the independent claim itself.
- **Method claims**: You may also want a parallel method claim (e.g., "A method of servicing a stock transport system... comprising disconnecting a first suction box from a shared suction line while maintaining suction to a second suction box...").
- **Drawings**: Patent claims of this type are typically supported by figures showing the coupling detail and box arrangement — I'd recommend sketching those out to make sure the claim language matches what's actually depicted.

Would you like me to draft a method claim, or expand the specification with alternative embodiments (e.g., different coupling types, or three-plus suction box arrangements)?

# Suction Box Arrangement for Print Unit Web Guidance

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates to a suction box arrangement for a printing press, and more particularly to a suction box configured for guiding a printed web through a print unit, incorporating a specifically oriented inlet opening, a transverse extension adapted to the web width, and features enabling improved access for maintenance and servicing.

---

## Background

In web-fed printing presses, particularly those employed in offset, flexographic, or gravure printing operations, printed webs must be guided through various sections of the print unit with minimal risk of smearing, marking, or otherwise damaging the freshly printed surface. Suction boxes are commonly employed to stabilize the web via a negative-pressure (vacuum) effect, drawing the web against a guide surface, roller, or perforated belt without direct mechanical contact with the printed side.

Conventional suction box arrangements, however, often suffer from several drawbacks:

1. The orientation of the air inlet opening relative to the web travel direction can create turbulence or uneven suction distribution across the web width, leading to flutter, wrinkling, or inconsistent tension.
2. The transverse (cross-web) dimensioning of the suction box is frequently fixed or difficult to adapt to different web widths, requiring separate tooling or full replacement of the unit for different job configurations.
3. Access to the interior of the suction box for cleaning, inspection, or repair is often restricted by the surrounding press frame components, requiring extensive disassembly and resulting in significant press downtime.

There exists a need for a suction box arrangement that addresses these limitations through improved inlet geometry, adaptable transverse extension, and enhanced serviceability.

---

## Summary of the Invention

According to the invention, a suction box arrangement for a print unit is provided, comprising:

- a suction box body defining an internal negative-pressure chamber;
- at least one inlet opening formed in a wall of the suction box body, the inlet opening being oriented at a defined angle relative to the web travel direction and/or relative to a longitudinal axis of the suction box, so as to promote uniform distribution of suction airflow across the web width and to reduce turbulent boundary effects near the box's longitudinal ends;
- a transverse extension of the suction box body that spans substantially the full operative width of the printed web, wherein the transverse extension is configured to be adjustable or modular, allowing adaptation to webs of varying width without requiring replacement of the entire suction box;
- one or more service openings, access panels, or hinged/removable wall sections formed in the suction box body, positioned to allow direct access to the interior chamber, suction openings, and associated ducting from an operator side of the print unit, without requiring removal of adjacent guide rollers or press frame components.

The combination of these features enables uniform web stabilization while significantly reducing maintenance time and complexity.

## Detailed Description

### 1. General Arrangement

Referring to the drawings (not reproduced here but referenced by numeral convention), the suction box arrangement (10) is disposed within a print unit (1) of a web-fed printing press, downstream and/or upstream of a printing couple, at a location where the printed web (W) passes over or adjacent to the suction box (10) to be guided along a defined path without physical contact between the printed image and a mechanical guide surface.

The suction box (10) comprises a housing (11) having a top wall (12), a bottom wall (13), two longitudinal side walls (14, 15) extending in the web travel direction (X), and two end walls (16, 17) extending transversely thereto, in the cross-web direction (Y). The housing (11) defines an internal chamber (18) that is connected via a duct (19) to a suction source, such as a blower or vacuum pump (20), which generates a negative pressure within the chamber (18) relative to ambient atmospheric pressure.

The top wall (12), facing the web (W), is provided with a plurality of perforations, slots, or a porous/perforated plate (21) through which air is drawn from the region adjacent the web (W) into the chamber (18), thereby generating a suction force that draws the web (W) toward the top wall (12) without direct contact, or with only minimal contact via a low-friction guide surface, belt, or roller arrangement disposed thereupon.

### 2. Inlet Opening Orientation

A distinguishing feature of the present arrangement is the orientation of the inlet opening (22) through which air enters the negative-pressure chamber (18) en route to the suction duct (19) and blower (20).

In contrast to conventional arrangements in which the inlet opening is formed perpendicular to the longitudinal axis (L) of the suction box or is aligned coaxially with the duct (19), the inlet opening (22) of the present invention is formed such that its central axis (A) is oriented at an oblique angle α relative to the longitudinal axis (L) of the suction box housing (11), the angle α being selected in the range of approximately 15° to 75°, and preferably between 30° and 60°.

This oblique orientation causes incoming air to be introduced into the chamber (18) with a directional component along the transverse (Y) direction, rather than purely along the longitudinal (X) or vertical (Z) direction. As a result, the air entering the chamber (18) is distributed more evenly across the full transverse extension of the chamber (18) before being drawn upward through the perforated top wall (12), thereby equalizing the suction pressure profile across the width of the web (W) and reducing localized zones of excessive or insufficient suction near the box ends (16, 17).

In a further embodiment, the inlet opening (22) is positioned asymmetrically along the longitudinal axis (L) of the suction box (10), for example nearer to one end wall (16) than the other end wall (17), in combination with an internal baffle or deflector plate (23) disposed within the chamber (18) proximate the inlet opening (22). The deflector plate (23) is angled so as to redirect the incoming airflow preferentially toward the more distal portions of the chamber (18), further promoting uniform pressure distribution.

In another embodiment, a plurality of inlet openings (22a, 22b, ...) are distributed along the length of the suction box (10), each oriented at a respective oblique angle, the angles being selected to progressively counteract the natural pressure gradient that would otherwise develop along the chamber (18) due to duct flow resistance.

### 3. Transverse Extension and Adaptability

The suction box housing (11) is configured with a transverse extension (i.e., the dimension along the Y-axis, corresponding to the cross-web direction) that is selected to correspond substantially to the full width of the printed web (W), or to the maximum web width for which the print unit (1) is rated.

In one embodiment, the suction box housing (11) is of modular construction, comprising a central housing segment (11a) and one or more end housing segments (11b, 11c) that are removably or slidably coupled to the central segment (11a), for example via flanged, telescoping, or dovetail-slide connections (24). By adding, removing, or repositioning the end segments (11b, 11c), the overall transverse extension of the suction box (10) can be adjusted to accommodate different web widths without requiring fabrication of an entirely new housing.

In a further embodiment, the transverse extension of the suction box (10) is adjustable via a telescoping side wall or end wall arrangement, wherein the end walls (16, 17) are slidably mounted relative to the top wall (12) and bottom wall (13) via guide rails (25) and are secured in a selected position by locking members (26), such as clamping screws, cam levers, or pneumatic clamps. Sealing strips or gaskets (27) disposed along the sliding interfaces maintain the negative-pressure integrity of the chamber (18) across the range of adjustment.

The perforated top wall (12), or the portion thereof exposed to the web (W), may similarly be provided in sections corresponding to the modular or telescoping extension, such that unused perforated sections beyond the active web width can be selectively closed off or masked, for example via a sliding cover plate (28) or a blanking insert, in order to prevent loss of suction efficiency due to air being drawn through regions not covered by the web (W).

### 4. Serviceability Features

To facilitate maintenance, cleaning, and inspection of the suction box arrangement (10), the housing (11) is provided with one or more service access features.

In one embodiment, at least one of the side walls (14, 15) or the bottom wall (13) is provided with a hinged access panel (30) mounted via a hinge (31) along one edge and secured in a closed position via a latch, quick-release fastener, or over-center clamp (32) along the opposite edge. Opening of the access panel (30) provides direct access to the interior chamber (18), including the inlet opening (22), deflector plate (23) (if present), and the underside of the perforated top wall (12), allowing for cleaning of accumulated dust, paper fibers, ink mist, or debris without requiring removal of the suction box (10) from the print unit (1) or disassembly of adjacent web-guide rollers.

In a further embodiment, the entire suction box housing (11), or a modular segment thereof, is mounted to the print unit frame (2) via a slide-out mounting arrangement (33), comprising rails (34) affixed to the frame (2) and corresponding slide elements (35) affixed to the housing (11), such that the suction box (10), or a portion thereof, can be withdrawn from its operative position in the machine direction or in the transverse direction for external servicing, and subsequently reinserted and relocated with repeatable positional accuracy via locating pins or detents (36).

In yet a further embodiment, the perforated top wall (12) is itself removably mounted to the housing (11), for example via a plurality of quick-release fasteners (37) or a hinged mounting along one longitudinal edge, such that the top wall (12) can be pivoted or lifted away from the housing (11) to expose the full interior of the chamber (18) for inspection or replacement of the perforated plate (21) due to wear, blockage, or damage.

The duct (19) connecting the chamber (18) to the blower (20) may further be provided with a quick-disconnect coupling (38), permitting rapid separation of the suction box (10) from the remainder of the pneumatic system for removal or servicing.

### 5. Optional Sensor Integration

In certain embodiments, the suction box arrangement (10) further comprises one or more pressure sensors (40) disposed within the chamber (18) at spaced-apart locations along the transverse extension, the sensors (40) being connected to a control unit (41) configured to monitor the uniformity of the negative pressure across the width of the chamber (18) and to adjust the blower (20) output, or to actuate a variable-position deflector plate (23) via an actuator (42), in order to maintain a target pressure profile, particularly in response to changes in the effective transverse extension resulting from adjustment of the modular or telescoping housing segments described above.
